transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2028-10-03 15:30 PDT
- Duration: 62 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Reyes (Redwood SE), Lena Park (Product), Rahul Iyer (CTO), Sofia Martinez (Infra), Tom Brooks (ML Eng)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
Zephyr is evaluating Redwood for a mix of customer-facing conversational features and backend content generation for email/notifications. Key decision factors are multilingual support (EN, ES, FR, JP), long-context handling (32k+ for multi-document threads), tool-calling for ERPs and search, and deployment model tradeoffs (hosted for speed vs dedicated/private for data residency and SLAs). Security/regulatory constraints include EU data residency for EU users and SAML SSO integration.

Topics (auto): model choices (open LLMs vs managed), context length, quantization/latency tradeoffs, tool-calling reliability, VPC/Private deployment feasibility, pricing/commits.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Great, hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood inference, and with me is Carlos our solutions engineer.
[00:10] Lena Park: Hey, thanks Maya, hi Carlos. We're excited, we kind of want to run through a few scenarios, high level questions first then get into the weeds.
[00:18] Carlos Reyes: Awesome. Could you kick off with the product use cases and traffic profile? That helps us pick models and routes.
[00:25] Rahul Iyer: Sure. Two broad buckets, one is real-time consumer chat in-app, low latency target around 200-400ms token emission ideally for short replies, multi-tenant across regions. Second is a backend composer for weekly newsletters and multi-doc summarization — those require longer context windows, sometimes 60k tokens for a full thread.
[00:48] Sofia Martinez: On infra constraints, EU data residency for EU users, plus we need SAML SSO and audit logs. We may prefer a private deployment for some regulated customers but want to understand cost tradeoffs.
[01:10] Maya Chen: Makes sense. For the chat path, a smaller open model or a quantized variant can hit latency and cost targets on Hosted; for the multi-doc summarization 60k context, we typically recommend dedicated or private with models supporting extended context — we have partner profiles for 64k/100k context models.
[01:36] Tom Brooks: Quick clarifying Q: when you say "partner profiles" you mean you host pre-quantized model variants? Is there any manual tuning on our side?
[01:44] Carlos Reyes: Good question. We ingest model artifacts and create optimized runtime profiles — kernel selection, KV cache tuning, and continuous batching policies. For quantized variants we can either use our curated quantizations or help you roll your own. Some customers do custom fine-tuning offline, that is fine, but not required for service.
[02:05] Rahul Iyer: What about tool calling? We need reliable tool-calls for internal ERP lookups and an external search microservice. Latency plus at-least-once semantics matter.
[02:18] Carlos Reyes: Redwood supports structured tool-calls and function calling. For reliability we recommend a combination: small synchronous calls for critical lookups and asynchronous retries via our routing policies for non-blocking tasks. Also you can pin fallback policies — e.g., if a hosted model variant isn't available, fallback to a lower-cost dedicated pool.
[02:40] Lena Park: Are there examples of customers doing multi-lingual + tool calling? We're worried about hallucinations when models switch languages.
[02:49] Maya Chen: Yes, we've seen that. Best practices: keep language signals explicit in the prompt, use eval suites per language, and tie quality monitoring to prompt sets so regressions are caught. We can run a quick eval across EN/ES/FR/JP during a pilot.
[03:10] Rahul Iyer: Speaking of pilots, we have legal asking about data retention and encryption. If we run Hosted, can we get per-tenant logs offloaded? Also KMS integration?
[03:22] Maya Chen: Hosted supports customer-level tenancy and can forward audit logs to your SIEM. We support KMS integrations and HSM-backed key options in Private. We'll attach the SOC2 pack and KMS docs after the call.
[03:35] Sofia Martinez: For Private, how self-managed is the control plane vs Redwood-managed? We want to know upgrade windows and rollback policies.
[03:43] Carlos Reyes: Private can be run with a customer-managed VPC and you can choose control plane visibility. We usually recommend Redwood manage the control plane in a VPC peering arrangement for easier upgrades; on-prem air-gapped is also an option but has longer maintenance windows. We'll share runbook snippets.
[03:59] Tom Brooks: Back to models — we're trying to decide between smaller open models with longer context via attention sliding windows, versus larger context models native to 64k. How do we weigh this?
[04:10] Carlos Reyes: Tradeoffs: smaller models + windowing/recency caches reduce cost but increase engineering work on chunking and retrieval. Native large-context models simplify prompt engineering but cost more per token and may have different latency characteristics. For summarization heavy workloads we usually see better developer velocity with native long-context models.
[04:36] Lena Park: Latency targets for chat — are they realistic on Hosted? We saw in your public benchmarks number like tail p95 at 600ms for certain models.
[04:45] Maya Chen: Benchmarks vary by model and region. For hosted if you need strict p95 latency <300ms we often recommend Dedicated or reserved capacity to avoid noisy neighbor effect and to tune batching. Hosted gives faster time-to-value but Dedicated gives predictable latencies.
[05:03] Rahul Iyer: OK, can you summarize cost levers? We want to build an ROI model.
[05:10] Carlos Reyes: Sure. Cost levers include: model family (size), context length (longer = more tokens), batching policies, KV/prefix caching (reduces repeated context cost), quantization (reduces GPU memory and can reduce price), and routing policies (use cheaper variants for noncritical traffic). Redwood Optimize suggests configuration and can simulate unit cost given your workload.
[05:36] Lena Park: Our ML team is also evaluating open model quality vs Anthropic/OpenAI — we prefer open models for transparency, but we need parity on instruction adherence. Any recs?
[05:48] Carlos Reyes: We maintain a catalog of curated open models with verified inference profiles. For instruction-following you'd want to look at distilled instruction-tuned variants or fine-tune on your instruction data. We can run a head-to-head eval on your sample prompts.
[06:03] Tom Brooks: About multilingual — do you recommend single multilingual model or per-language models? We have heavy Spanish and Japanese traffic.
[06:13] Maya Chen: If you need high-quality Japanese, often a dedicated JP-optimized model is better. Multilingual models are convenient but sometimes underperform in low-resource languages. We usually suggest a hybrid: multilingual default + language-specific model for priority locales.
[06:30] Rahul Iyer: Any constraints for large KV caches with 60k contexts? Storage and eviction policies?
[06:38] Carlos Reyes: The runtime supports KV eviction policies and shard-aware caching; large contexts increase memory but we handle persistent KV cache to disk and warm-up strategies. There are tuning knobs: how long to keep cache, segmented eviction for per-user history, etc.
[06:58] Lena Park: Can you give a concrete pilot plan? We want metrics: latency, p95, cost per request, quality scores per language, tool-call reliability.
[07:06] Maya Chen: Recommended pilot: 2-week micro-pilot. Week 1: onboard with Hosted using a 32k model variant for chat and run controlled traffic for latency and quality. Week 2: spin up a Dedicated pool for the long-context summarization tests (64k model) and run end-to-end tool-calling reliability tests. Deliverables: perf spreadsheet, quality eval CSV, incident/reliability notes.
[07:34] Tom Brooks: That sounds good. About billing and commitments — Dedicated requires a min commit? What's the step from Hosted to Dedicated?
[07:43] Maya Chen: Dedicated typically has monthly reserved capacity commitments; minimum depends on config but we can design a small starter pool for a pilot at reduced commitment. Transitioning from Hosted to Dedicated is straightforward — same API surface, just a different routing policy.
[07:58] Rahul Iyer: Any red flags from your side on our architecture? We're thinking of doing on-prem for EU subset and Hosted elsewhere.
[08:06] Carlos Reyes: That hybrid model is common. We just want to confirm network topology for private links and egress patterns. Also ask Legal about export controls for model artifacts if you bring models on-prem. We can help with that checklist.
[08:21] Sofia Martinez: Security note: we need role-based access control for ops teams and per-route logging. Can Redwood expose token-level RBAC?
[08:29] Maya Chen: Yes, RBAC and token scoping is supported; Console can show per-route token usage and you can set route-based quotas. We'll include screenshots in the follow-up security doc.
[08:42] Lena Park: A few questions from the product team: can your runtime do partial streaming for long completions so that UX gets early tokens?
[08:51] Carlos Reyes: Yes we support streaming chunked responses and partial KV flush to start emitting tokens while the backend completes further computation. That helps UX for long-gen tasks.
[09:03] Tom Brooks: Regarding quantization — any accuracy regressions observed for JP? We worry char-level tokenization getting worse.
[09:12] Carlos Reyes: Some quantization strategies can degrade fine-grained languages; we recommend testing quantized variants in a controlled eval. If you need we can do per-language WER/quality gating.
[09:26] Rahul Iyer: What about fallbacks? If a model hits capacity do you circuit-break or degrade to smaller model? We need predictable user experience.
[09:35] Maya Chen: Redwood supports policy-based fallback: you can fallback by latency, cost, or region. For consumer chat you'd likely fallback to a smaller but faster variant with a user-visible "reduced fidelity" flag so your app can handle it gracefully.
[09:52] Lena Park: Can we instrument prompt-level cost attribution for product analytics?
[10:00] Carlos Reyes: Yes, token-level cost and routing logs are available and can be exported to BigQuery/Snowflake. That helps ROI dashboards.
[10:12] Sofia Martinez: Any compliance packs for EU hosting and GDPR concerns?
[10:18] Maya Chen: We'll share our GDPR whitepaper and EU region hosting documentation. For Private, customers often keep EU data on-prem or in an EU cloud region we operate in partnership.
[10:30] Rahul Iyer: How long do upgrades take if we're on Private? We need SLAs and maintenance windows.
[10:36] Carlos Reyes: Private upgrades depend on deployment topology. If Redwood manages the control plane in your VPC, upgrades are staged and we provide rollback points. We can commit to maintenance windows and an SLA in an enterprise contract.
[10:52] Lena Park: OK, let's cover the pilot artifacts again and responsibilities.
[10:58] Maya Chen: Recap: Redwood -> send security docs, pricing, and pilot template. SE -> run context-size perf estimate and propose Dedicated starter config. Customer -> provide sample prompts, tool-call patterns, and define success metrics (latency, p95, quality per language).
[11:16] Tom Brooks: We'll assemble prompts and a small corpus for the weekend.
[11:22] Rahul Iyer: And we want a one-hour SE deep-dive next week to look at perf numbers and API integration details.
[11:29] Maya Chen: Perfect, we'll schedule that. Any other open Qs?
[11:34] Sofia Martinez: Nothing else on my end, just small note — can we get an example runbook for incident response?
[11:39] Carlos Reyes: Yes, we'll include a runbook snippet and escalation contacts.
[11:44] Lena Park: Thanks everyone, that was helpful.
[11:47] Maya Chen: Thanks folks, we'll follow up with the materials and a calendar invite for the deep dive.
[11:54] End of recording.
